item.title: Reuse existing money helpers for Decimal arithmetic
item.description: When implementing monetary calculations, use the project's existing money utilities (to_money, round_money, ZERO) instead of raw Decimal operations.
item.content: Inspect ledgerly/money.py and sibling functions like line_total/invoice_total to learn the rounding and coercion conventions. Wrap unit_price with to_money, seed sums with ZERO, and round the final result with round_money to stay consistent with the rest of the codebase.

item.title: Guard division by zero before computing averages
item.description: For weighted-average functions, compute the denominator first and return the zero constant when it is zero to avoid ZeroDivisionError.
item.content: Sum quantities (or weights) up front; if the total is 0, return ZERO immediately. This handles empty invoices and zero-quantity lines without special-casing each line.

item.title: Read the target test and models before implementing
item.description: Before writing a new function, inspect the existing test file and dataclass models to confirm signatures, field names, and expected return types.
item.content: Cat tests/test_<feature>.py and ledgerly/models.py to learn exact field names (e.g., line.quantity, line.unit_price) and expected equality semantics (e.g., Decimal == int). This avoids mismatched attribute names and type annotations.

item.title: Reuse existing money/error helpers for validation
item.description: When implementing a billing function, delegate normalization and error signaling to the module's existing helpers rather than reimplementing them.
item.content: Use the repo's `to_money`/`ZERO`/`round_money` helpers to normalize amounts and compare against zero, and raise the project's `BillingError(code, message)` with short machine-readable codes. This matches existing conventions and keeps error codes consistent with hidden tests.

item.title: Guard bool when validating integer inputs
item.description: Python's `bool` is a subclass of `int`, so `isinstance(x, int)` accepts `True`/`False`; explicitly reject bools for integer-only parameters.
item.content: For positive-integer validation write `isinstance(quantity, bool) or not isinstance(quantity, int) or quantity <= 0`. This catches floats, strings, and booleans that would otherwise slip through or be silently coerced.

item.title: Read tests and sibling modules before implementing
item.description: Exploring the target file, its models, error types, and the provided tests first let the implementation match expected signatures and conventions on the first try.
item.content: Before writing code, cat the target module, related models/money/errors modules, and any test file for the function. Then run the full test suite plus a manual edge-case script (zero, negative, float, bool, wrong state) to confirm behavior before submitting.

item.title: Reuse existing time/error helpers for datetime logic
item.description: Before implementing date arithmetic, grep the codebase for existing utilities like ensure_utc and BillingError and reuse them for consistency.
item.content: Search for sibling modules (e.g. subscriptions.py, clock.py, errors.py) that already do similar period math. Reusing ensure_utc for tz normalization and BillingError for validation keeps behavior consistent and satisfies hidden tests expecting those error codes.

item.title: Validate numeric fields defensively before arithmetic
item.description: Guard against bool, non-int, and non-positive period values before using them in timedelta math.
item.content: Check `isinstance(x, bool)` first (bool is an int subclass), then `isinstance(x, int)`, then `x <= 0`, raising the project's domain error. This prevents silent wrong results or TypeError from timedelta.

item.title: Use floor-division formula for strictly-after recurrence
item.description: Compute the first occurrence strictly after a timestamp with `n = (after - start) // length + 1`, handling the before-start case separately.
item.content: For events at start + k*length (k>=1), the strictly-after answer is `start + ((after - start) // length + 1) * length`. If `after < start`, return `start + length` directly. Verify boundary cases (after == start, after == a renewal) with a quick script.

item.title: Check idempotency key before any state validation
item.description: Money-moving operations must short-circuit on a repeated idempotency_key before validating payment state, so retries return the original result instead of raising.
item.content: Accept keyword-only `idempotency_key=None`; first scan `audit.events(<event>)` for a matching key and return the original record unchanged. Only then validate state/amounts, and include `idempotency_key` in the audit entry you write.

item.title: Apply approval thresholds to support-initiated money movements
item.description: Refunds/credits above the finance threshold require a second approver, exposed as an optional keyword-only `approved_by=None`.
item.content: Define a module-level threshold constant (e.g. `APPROVAL_THRESHOLD = to_money("500.00")`); amounts at or below it need no approval, above it raise `BillingError("approval_required")` when `approved_by` is None. Keep the parameter optional so existing callers still work.

item.title: Mirror sibling module conventions when implementing a stub
item.description: Before writing a new function, read sibling modules (payments, audit, money, clock) and existing tests to copy their money rounding, error codes, and audit patterns.
item.content: Use `to_money`/`round_money`/`ZERO` for all arithmetic, `ensure_utc` for timestamps, and `BillingError(code, detail)` for failures; record an audit event with the same shape as neighboring operations so hidden tests and conventions line up.

item.title: Reuse existing money helpers instead of raw round()
item.description: When implementing monetary functions, delegate to the repo's existing to_money/round_money helpers rather than Python's round() to match conventions and precision.
item.content: Read sibling modules (invoice.py, money.py) to find canonical helpers like to_money and round_money, then build new pricing functions on top of them. This keeps Decimal handling and cent-rounding consistent across the codebase.

item.title: Validate numeric inputs against bool and type before arithmetic
item.description: Guard against bools and unexpected types when accepting numeric parameters, since bool is an int subclass and would silently pass range checks.
item.content: Check `isinstance(x, bool) or not isinstance(x, (int, Decimal))` before converting to Decimal, then enforce range bounds. Raise the project's domain error (e.g. BillingError with a stable code) rather than ValueError for invalid business inputs.

item.title: Read existing tests to infer expected return types and error conventions
item.description: Inspect the test suite and sibling modules before implementing to learn expected types, error classes, and edge-case behavior.
item.content: Tests like test_tax.py reveal that add_tax should return a Decimal comparable to ints, and core tests show BillingError usage. Align signatures, return types, and error codes with these signals before writing code.

item.title: Check team conventions before implementing money-moving operations
item.description: The first attempt was rejected because it omitted the required keyword-only idempotency_key parameter that all payment/credit/invoice balance operations must support.
item.content: Before implementing any operation that moves money or changes a payment, credit or invoice balance, scan sibling modules and the README/CHANGELOG for cross-cutting conventions (idempotency, audit, rounding). These conventions are often not visible in the target function's stub or its tests, so passing local tests is not sufficient evidence of correctness.

item.title: Implement idempotency by checking audit events first
item.description: Idempotent operations must look up prior audit entries by key before validating state, and return the original result without reapplying the operation.
item.content: Add `*, idempotency_key: str | None = None` to the signature, then at the very top of the function iterate `audit.events(<event_type>)` and return the original record if any entry's `idempotency_key` matches. Only after that check should you validate state (e.g. status == 'authorized') and mutate. Always include `idempotency_key` in the audit entry you write, even when None.

item.title: Match existing module idioms for validation, time and errors
item.description: Reuse the module's established helpers (ensure_utc, BillingError with code/message, audit.record) rather than inventing new patterns.
item.content: Read the sibling functions in the same file (e.g. authorize) and mirror their structure: normalize datetimes with ensure_utc, raise BillingError(code, message) for invalid states, and record an audit event with the same field naming. This keeps behavior consistent and satisfies hidden tests that assert on error codes and audit payloads.
